common_name: Blue Mouse Ears Hosta (Miniature Thick-Leaved Blue Hosta)

planting.note: Plant divisions in early fall or spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Blue Mouse Ears is a true miniature hosta, staying tiny for years, which makes it a favorite for rock gardens, troughs, and the front edge of a shade border.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Blue Mouse Ears won the American Hosta Growers Association Hosta of the Year award and remains one of the most popular miniature hosta cultivars, forming a tight, slow-spreading mound of thick, rounded, powdery blue-green leaves that keep their color and substance better through summer heat than many thinner-leaved hostas. Its small size and unusually slug-resistant, thick foliage make it a favorite for containers, rock gardens, and the front of a shaded border where larger hostas would be out of scale. Lavender flowers appear on short scapes in summer. It divides easily but slowly, so mature clumps take a few years to bulk up enough to split.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; Citronelle's bright chartreuse-yellow color is most vivid in some morning sun with afternoon shade, since heavy shade dulls the color toward green.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade with some morning sun to bring out the brightest foliage color. Citronelle is one of the most vividly colored yellow-leaved heuchera cultivars, producing a dense mound of glowing chartreuse-yellow leaves that light up a shaded border and pair strikingly with dark-leaved companions like Caramel or Obsidian heuchera, purple-leaved heucherella, or blue hostas. Small, airy sprays of pale flowers rise on wiry stems above the foliage in early summer, though the plant is grown primarily for its foliage color rather than its blooms. Divide the clump every few years in spring as the center begins to heave or thin, replanting vigorous outer sections.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Visions is a compact Astilbe chinensis selection that tolerates somewhat drier soil and more sun than most astilbe cultivars, though consistent moisture still gives the best results.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Visions is a compact Astilbe chinensis cultivar producing dense, bottlebrush-like plumes of rich raspberry-pink flowers in mid-to-late summer above glossy, dark green, finely cut foliage, blooming somewhat later in the season than many Arendsii-type astilbe cultivars. Its Chinese astilbe parentage gives it better tolerance of drier soil and more sun exposure than most astilbes, though it still performs best with consistent moisture and appreciates deep shade and heavy mulch through the hottest part of a zone 9 summer. The dried flower plumes remain attractive well after bloom, and clumps can be divided every three to four years in early spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Bridal Veil Astilbe (Classic White Arendsii Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Bridal Veil requires consistently moist soil and does not tolerate prolonged drought, so mulch heavily and irrigate through dry spells, especially in zone 9 summer heat.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade. Bridal Veil is one of the classic Georg Arends astilbe hybrids, producing airy, arching plumes of pure white flowers in early summer above finely cut, glossy green compound foliage, a graceful contrast to the deeper reds and pinks of many other astilbe cultivars. Like other astilbes it thrives in the consistently moist, humus-rich, shaded conditions found near streams, ponds, and under trees, and struggles if allowed to dry out, especially through zone 9 summer heat where deep shade and heavy mulch are important for success. The dried seed plumes remain attractive for weeks after bloom, and dividing the clump every three to four years in early spring keeps it vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Raspberry Splash flowers very early in spring, often among the first shade perennials to bloom, and its heavily silver-spotted leaves provide season-long foliage interest afterward.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade. Raspberry Splash produces clusters of small, funnel-shaped raspberry-pink flowers in very early spring, among the first blooms in the shade garden each year, held above heavily silver-spotted, softly bristled leaves that continue to provide strong foliage texture and contrast for the rest of the growing season. Like other lungworts it combines beautifully with hostas, ferns, and hellebores in a woodland border, and it tolerates fairly dry shade once established better than many shade perennials, though consistent moisture during establishment gives the best results. Divide congested clumps in early fall every few years to maintain vigor and refresh the planting.
